generator_view.scenario: A listener is preparing to buy a first serious pair of headphones and wants mechanism homework rather than another price-tier ranking. They keep seeing wired, Bluetooth, Bluetooth 5.x, Bluetooth Low Energy, LE Audio, A2DP, codec, DAC, amplifier, DSP, and lossless language used as though it all meant the same thing. The available material includes standards-history and protocol pages, audio-coding and playback-chain pages, two current catalog architecture examples, and two community discussions about Bluetooth sound and converting wired IEMs for wireless use.
generator_view.target: Explain the supported evolution of Bluetooth audio from early standards organization and Classic stereo transport deployment through the Wibree-to-Bluetooth-Low-Energy lineage and the LE Audio and LC3 transition. Then compare the complete wired and wireless playback paths so a first-time buyer can verify the exact endpoints and modes that may create audible differences. Preserve history-versus-deployment, format-versus-implementation, seller-page, and community-experience boundaries; do not manufacture an A2DP release year or a universal wired-better verdict.

query_requirements.text: Give a source-bounded chronology from the Bluetooth SIG and Classic AVDTP and A2DP role and deployment evidence through Wibree, Bluetooth Low Energy, LE Audio, and LC3, explicitly distinguishing organization history, transport role, operating-system deployment, and later evolution.

Compare the complete wired and wireless signal paths, including source coding, negotiated transport and codec, decoding, DAC, amplifier, DSP, power state, transducer, fit, and modular receiver examples, while treating community comments as scoped experiences.

Conclude with an operational first-purchase checklist for exact source, operating system, Classic or LE Audio support, actually negotiated profile and codec, mode-specific electronics, output compatibility, matched loudness, and separate sound, latency, stability, battery, microphone, and convenience judgments; avoid a universal wired-better or version-badge claim.

State the bounded conclusion, explain why neither connection label universally determines sound quality, and identify when missing exact endpoint or mode-specific information prevents a purchase prediction.

accepted_phrases: The supported chronology begins with the Bluetooth SIG as the standards organization founded in September 1998, but that organizational date is not an A2DP launch date. The protocol source explains that AVDTP is used by the advanced audio distribution profile to stream music to stereo headsets over L2CAP, while the stack source supplies later operating-system deployment observations for Mac OS X 10.5 and Windows 8; role and deployment must not be converted into a manufactured first-release year. A distinct low-energy lineage runs from Wibree's public release in October 2006, through the June 2007 agreement to include it in a future Bluetooth specification, to completed Bluetooth 4.0 integration in early 2010. LE Audio was announced in January 2020 on Bluetooth 5.2 or 5.3, introduced LC3 as its default codec, and was announced complete on 12 July 2022. LC3 is described as a Bluetooth SIG BLE-audio codec introduced around Bluetooth 5.2 and succeeding SBC, but its comparative quality passage is based on subjective testing and includes a disputed comparison, so neither LC3 nor a newer Bluetooth version guarantees a better result for every implementation or listener.

Compare complete paths rather than connection labels. Start with the file or streamed representation and any lossy coding, then identify the negotiated transport and codec, decoding, digital-to-analog conversion, amplification, optional DSP, and the headphone transducer and fit. The coding source separates a format from the algorithms of a codec implementation and says lossy coding irretrievably removes information; the DAC source says a digital stream returns to analog before amplification and reproduction; and the amplifier source shows that distortion, output impedance, frequency response, and DSP can vary by implementation. A cable avoids a radio transport stage, but it does not make every source, DAC, amplifier, DSP setting, or transducer identical. A wireless path may add transport coding or use internal electronics, yet that does not prove an audible loss in every endpoint pair. The community pages show both configuration-dependent reports and modular wired-IEM-to-Bluetooth arrangements; they motivate exact-path verification and matched listening, not prevalence or a universal wired-versus-wireless verdict. Seller pages showing a 3.5 millimetre Bluetooth receiver and a dual-mode headset are architecture observations only, not history or controlled fidelity tests.
